idiom_name: one module as the monitor: __all__ as the enumerated surface, private module state, fail-closed decision
implementation_notes: Python enforces no privacy, so the realization is a discipline expressed through module structure: the monitor is one module whose only public names are the mediated operations, listed in __all__, whose decision state lives in leading-underscore module globals, and which depends on nothing but the policy interface and a single _check function that returns False whenever it cannot decide. Name mangling (__name inside a class becomes _Class__name) is not privacy either - it only prevents accidental collisions - so it belongs nowhere in the trust argument. The value of the single module is verifiability: the whole trusted core is one file whose public surface is the __all__ list, and the test suite iterates that same list, so adding a mediated operation changes both in the same commit.
pitfalls: Leading underscores and __all__ are conventions read by humans: any imported module can call monitor._check or rebind monitor._POLICY, and name mangling only rewrites the attribute name, so in-process enforcement in Python is advisory.

Monkey patching is the normal way Python is extended: a plugin that replaces _check, a sitecustomize module, or a wrapper that swaps the module in sys.modules disables the monitor without editing a line of it.

Returning the stored object, or a shallow copy that shares mutable sub-objects, hands the caller a reference that mutates state the monitor believes it controls; return deep copies or immutable views.
Import order is part of the trust boundary: if the policy is imported lazily, a decision can run before it exists - which is exactly the state that must fail closed instead of defaulting open.

variants.name: Runtime audit hook mediation (sys.addaudithook)
variants.idiom_name: sys.addaudithook() mediating runtime events (cannot be removed once installed)
variants.implementation_notes: PEP 578 gives the runtime its own mediation surface: sys.addaudithook() installs a hook that CPython calls for events raised throughout the interpreter and standard library - open, socket.connect, subprocess.Popen, ctypes.dlopen, compile, import, sys._getframe and the rest of the audit events table - and hooks cannot be removed or replaced once added; a hook that raises aborts the operation. Hooks added from C are global, hooks added from Python belong to the current interpreter, so an embedder can install the monitor before any application code runs. What it is not: the PEP says explicitly that this is not a sandbox. The hook sees runtime events rather than object-level intent, a denial is an exception (or process termination), and anything below the interpreter - a C extension, a build with auditing disabled - can act without raising the events. Use it to mediate resource acquisition (files, sockets, processes, native code) and the module monitor for object-level decisions.
pitfalls: An installed hook is permanent for the process: a slow or wrong hook can only be fixed by restarting, so keep it allocation-light and never raise for events outside the policy.

Hooks run with the GIL held on the thread that raised the event, so doing I/O, taking locks or logging to a slow sink inside the hook stalls the program and can deadlock against a lock the audited operation needs.

Coverage is a runtime property, not a language guarantee: builds with auditing disabled, C extensions that bypass the audited path and events added in later Python versions all move the surface - pin the version and test the event list you rely on.
Denial semantics are blunt: the exception aborts the operation for every caller at once, and a denial cannot be attributed to a decision id unless the monitor records it.
